_doc: Worked examples the book uses to ground abstract claims. `illustrates` holds mechanism slugs or typed ids; `illustratesConcepts` / `illustratesClaims` hold concept / claim slugs (all become `illustrates` edges). `appearsIn` lists chapters. `evidence` is one sentence on how far the case can be trusted. Card-layer fields (`plain`, `passages`, `related`, `autolink`) as in concepts.json; the card body lives in content/cases/<id>.md.

caseStudies.label: The telephone game
caseStudies.summary: Ten kids pass a sentence around a circle; the output barely resembles the input. The canonical pure-transport intuition — but note that the game forces every player to pass, removing the selection step that real social networks have.
caseStudies.plain: Whisper a sentence around a circle of ten children and it comes out garbled, which shows how retelling alone wears an idea down.

caseStudies.label: Hammer of the Witches vs. Copernicus
caseStudies.summary: Same press technology, two generations apart (1486 and 1543). The Hammer ran through edition after edition; De revolutionibus was famously slow to sell (Koestler called it 'the book that nobody read'; Gingerich later showed specialists read it closely, which sharpens rather than weakens the contrast in reach). Pure-transport reads it as compressed-vs-complex. Selection reads it as identical transport cost with massively different fitness against contemporary criteria — fear, urgency, action affordance.
caseStudies.plain: The same early printing presses produced a witch-hunting manual that ran through edition after edition and an astronomy book by Copernicus that reached only specialists.

passages.section: Hammer of the Witches, properly this time

caseStudies.label: matplotlib vs. seaborn
caseStudies.summary: matplotlib: general, powerful, hard to use. seaborn: opinionated abstraction, lower ceiling, broader access. The 'software stratification' pattern — same trade-off shows up in religions, political platforms, scientific popularization.
caseStudies.plain: One charting tool lets you do anything but is hard to learn; another is easy because it has already made most choices for you.

passages.section: What the curve is, and what it isn't

caseStudies.label: Astrology
caseStudies.summary: Astronomical positions are real measurements; the interpretive framework is invented. Never survived consensus (never went through it), injected directly at curation and meme stages. Canonical example of manufactured content propagating through the same channels as measured content.
caseStudies.plain: Horoscopes use real star and planet positions, but the idea that those positions shape your personality was made up and never tested.

passages.section: Case 4: Astrology — manufactured content in the pipeline

caseStudies.label: 'Scientists say X' headline
caseStudies.summary: A 20-year paper compresses to a meme within a week. Pure-transport says lossy hops; selection says the headline writer chose the highest-fitness finding, not the most load-bearing one. Both pipelines are operating.
caseStudies.plain: Twenty years of careful research can reach the public as one confident headline, with every caveat and condition left behind.

passages.section: What a message is made of

caseStudies.label: Bitcoin: 'internet money' vs. full technical description
caseStudies.summary: 'Bitcoin is internet money' requires almost no preconditions. The full settlement-layer description requires five or six. Same object, two forms — only the compressed form has a chance of reaching unprepared receivers.
caseStudies.plain: Calling Bitcoin "internet money" leaves out nearly everything that matters, yet it is the only description short enough to reach newcomers.

caseStudies.label: Power posing — the meme that survived its own corrective
caseStudies.summary: Carney/Cuddy/Yap 2010 reported that 'high-power' poses raised testosterone, lowered cortisol, and improved risk-task performance. Published in Psychological Science, popularized via Cuddy's 70M-view TED talk and the book Presence. Ranehill et al. 2015 failed to replicate; Carney publicly disavowed the work in 2016. Within the field the original is treated as a canonical replication-crisis case; in popular culture the meme keeps spreading, because the corrective signal has worse curation fitness than the original. Made-to-meme + meme-survived-the-correction is the chapter's prototype case.
caseStudies.plain: A small 2010 study said power poses change your hormones; it failed to replicate, its lead author disowned it, and people still repeat it.

passages.section: Case 1: Power posing — all the way to meme

caseStudies.label: Arsenic-life (Wolfe-Simon et al. 2010) — died at consensus
caseStudies.summary: December 2010 Science paper claiming GFAJ-1 bacteria could substitute arsenic for phosphorus in DNA. NASA press conference; initial curation began. Within days the microbiologist Rosie Redfield posted a detailed critique; Science published eight technical comments in 2011 and, in 2012, two independent refutations showing that GFAJ-1's DNA held no arsenate and the original signal came from arsenic contamination. Consensus settled to negative inside eighteen months. The meme barely propagated past the first press cycle because the consensus gate caught the variant before curation could compound it. The book's worked example of the consensus stage working as designed.
caseStudies.plain: In 2010 NASA-funded scientists announced a bacterium built with arsenic in its DNA, and other scientists disproved it before the story could take hold.

caseStudies.label: Stanford Prison Experiment correctives — died at curation
caseStudies.summary: Zimbardo's 1971 SPE ran the pipeline cleanly to meme — textbooks, films, public-intellectual platform. 2018 Ben Blum reporting and Le Texier's 2018/2019 archival work showed Zimbardo coached guards and the famous prisoner breakdown was performed; consensus within social psychology accepted the methodological critique. The corrective passed measurement, analysis, and consensus — and died at curation. Textbooks still teach SPE; pop psychology still cites it; films are not being re-cut. The book's worked example of corrective signal failing at curation even when consensus has ratified it.
caseStudies.plain: The famous 1971 prison experiment was shown to be coached and partly staged, yet textbooks and introductory courses still teach the original story.

passages.section: Case 3: Stanford Prison Experiment — the correction died at curation

caseStudies.label: Latin Mass vs. vernacular liturgy
caseStudies.summary: Pre-Vatican-II Catholicism: the Latin Mass is high optionality, low access — ritual carries a great deal of doctrinal precision, with centuries of qualification behind it; full participation requires a trained reader of the apparatus. The vernacular reform shifted to high access, lower precision — local-language liturgy that the broader laity can participate in, with some of the specific commitments the Latin form encoded arriving in language general enough to be read several ways. Optionality-vs-access trade-off in religion; the example of a tradition scaling past its founding community by making the trade through an institutional split, with the high-optionality form kept by a smaller specialist community while the high-access form reaches the wider audience.
caseStudies.plain: When the Catholic Mass moved from Latin to local languages, far more people could take part, at some cost in doctrinal precision.

passages.section: What the curve is, and what it isn't

caseStudies.label: A Brief History of Time
caseStudies.summary: Hawking's 1988 popularization of general relativity, quantum mechanics, and cosmology — written for readers with no physics background. Hawking's editor cut every equation past E=mc², and the book is full of choices about which apparatus to skip and which analogy to substitute for which equation. It sold more than 25 million copies; the papers it popularized have been read in full by a tiny fraction of that, mostly specialists. Optionality-vs-access trade in scientific popularization, with the same shape as software stratification: the popular form gains reach by trading the precision the technical form preserves.
caseStudies.plain: Stephen Hawking reached millions of readers by cutting nearly every equation from his physics book, trading exactness for reach.

passages.section: The same curve, at design time

caseStudies.label: Statutes vs. plain-language legal summaries
caseStudies.summary: A statute drafted by professional legislative counsel encodes precision through scope-defined clauses, defined-term interactions, and 'shall/may/subject to' constructions whose load-bearing work is invisible to non-lawyers. A plain-language summary of the same statute is accessible but wrong about the edge cases the original carefully handled. The legal apparatus is structurally committed to both ends of the curve simultaneously — the statute is preservation, the summary is access — with a professional class (lawyers) doing the per-case translation between them. The cleanest institutional bridge in the book's optionality-vs-access examples, and the one whose access is most explicitly wealth-gated.
caseStudies.plain: A one-line summary of a law is easy to read and right about the usual case, but wrong about edge cases the full text handles.

passages.section: What the curve is, and what it isn't

caseStudies.label: The Voyager Golden Record
caseStudies.summary: The book's illustration of Hofstadter's three-layer model of a message. A record launched into deep space with no shared context to assume: the recorded sounds and images are the inner message, the playback diagrams etched on the cover are the outer message, and the artifact's evident designed-ness is the frame message. The rare case where all three layers had to be shipped together.
caseStudies.plain: A record sent into deep space had to carry its own playing instructions, because nobody could assume the finder would know anything.

passages.section: What a message is made of

caseStudies.label: COVID mask guidance — a reversal read as a lie
caseStudies.summary: In early 2020 the CDC and WHO advised the public not to wear masks, bundling a genuine wish to preserve scarce medical masks with an early droplet-over-aerosol read of the evidence; on April 3, 2020 the CDC reversed to recommend cloth coverings as aerosol transmission became clearer. That is a field updating on evidence. The bridge zone shipped it as two confident slogans, "masks don't work" then "masks work," with the decoding key (the supply motive, the provisional evidence) stripped, so the reversal read not as science working but as experts lying or flip-flopping. The inversion regime operating on institutional credibility itself, and the case that did the most public-trust damage.
caseStudies.plain: Health agencies changed their mask advice as evidence came in, but the public heard two flat slogans and concluded the experts had lied.
caseStudies.evidence: The book's own framing of the episode; a primary source for it is still to be cited.

caseStudies.label: Nutrition science — forty years of monocausal reversals
caseStudies.summary: Fat, then low-fat, then carbs, then sugar, then ultra-processed food: a forty-year sequence in which the field says "it's complicated and confounded" and the bridge zone ships a confident single-cause story on repeat. Each reversal is a real finding stripped of its hedges and conditions and sold as a clean actionable line, leaving the audience with a working model of nutrition worse than none. The specialist consensus was itself more contested than a clean story admits (food-industry conflicts run through nutrition epidemiology), but the whiplash the public experienced is a bridge-zone artifact, not a property of the science.
caseStudies.plain: For forty years the public has been handed one confident dietary villain after another, while the science kept saying it was complicated.
caseStudies.evidence: The book's own framing of the episode; a primary source for it is still to be cited.

caseStudies.label: Monetary policy in the financial press
caseStudies.summary: Financial-press coverage of monetary policy collapses aggregates, velocity, and transmission mechanisms into "the Fed is printing money." This is where the political economy of attention bites hardest, because some outlets are owned by interests with positions on what policy should be, so the compression is not only lossy but directional. Monetary policy is genuinely full of paradigm wars, so the specialist consensus is contested too; the point is that the bridge-zone product is systematically wrong about the technical distinctions in a direction that serves its owners.
caseStudies.plain: Coverage of central banking boils a technical subject down to 'the Fed is printing money', and some of the outlets doing it have a stake in the answer.

passages.section: Where the political economy hits hardest

caseStudies.evidence: The book's own framing of the episode; a primary source for it is still to be cited.

caseStudies.label: Common-law courts as a curation institution
caseStudies.summary: Common-law courts run on generationally trained judges (a multi-decade consumer-key substrate), precedent as preservation, transparent written provenance, and redundant independent jurisdictions, all publicly funded. Read through the book's design principles, they hold funding-decoupling and consumer-key defense the longest and do correspondingly well. Their redundancy only works while the jurisdictions stay genuinely independent, which political capture of appointments erodes: the failure mode the principles predict.
caseStudies.plain: Common-law courts have kept hard knowledge alive for centuries by training judges for decades, writing everything down, and being paid for by the public.
caseStudies.evidence: The book's own framing of the episode; a primary source for it is still to be cited.

caseStudies.label: Stack Overflow — curation without funding decoupling
caseStudies.summary: Stack Overflow had strong reputation-weighted curation and auditable provenance but was never decoupled from the attention market (ad-supported and venture-backed from its 2008 launch). When LLMs began answering its questions directly, readers took the compressed model answer instead of the curated community one, traffic fell sharply after 2022, and with no funding reserve it had nothing to ride out the shock. The case that shows curation and provenance are not enough without the funding principle, and Chapter 11's worst case landing on a real curation layer.
caseStudies.plain: A programming Q&A site with strong quality control lost its audience when AI began answering the same questions, and it had no funding to fall back on.
caseStudies.evidence: The book's own framing of the episode; a primary source for it is still to be cited.

caseStudies.label: The Columbia slide
caseStudies.summary: During the 2003 Columbia mission, Boeing engineers briefed NASA managers on possible foam-strike damage with slides whose key caveats were buried in nested bullets under a reassuring headline, while the test data covered far smaller debris. The Columbia Accident Investigation Board (report p. 191) adopted Edward Tufte's analysis and noted that NASA officials often supplied slides in place of technical reports. It shows a presentation format making sustained argument costly and a caveat easy to miss.
caseStudies.evidence: Officially endorsed (the accident board adopted Tufte's analysis), but a single case in which the slide was one factor among many organizational causes.
caseStudies.plain: Engineers briefed NASA on possible shuttle damage with bullet-point slides, and the layout buried the caveats that mattered most.

passages.section: A slide that could not say it

caseStudies.label: Scientific forestry and the Normalbaum
caseStudies.summary: From about 1765 to 1800, Prussian and Saxon foresters defined a standardized tree (the Normalbaum), then cleared underbrush, reduced species often to monoculture and planted in rows, replacing forests that were about three-quarters broadleaf largely with Norway spruce or Scotch pine. The first rotation grew well; after the second, Scott quotes production losses of 20 to 30 percent over two or three generations, and the word Waldsterben (forest death) entered German. It shows a simplified record being used to remake the reality it described, and the remade reality failing.
caseStudies.evidence: A historical case study from James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State; interpretive evidence built on documented detail, which cannot be replicated the way an experiment can.
caseStudies.plain: German foresters replanted their woods to match a table of timber yields, and after one good harvest the simplified forests began to fail.

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory
What a framework does to a thought

caseStudies.label: Black-Scholes and the option market
caseStudies.summary: Donald MacKenzie identifies three phases for the Black-Scholes-Merton option-pricing model: prices fit it poorly from 1973 to 1976, converged on it from 1976 to summer 1987 as traders used it (partly through arbitrage), and departed from it after the October 1987 crash with a persistent volatility skew. The model's own parameter, implied volatility, became the market's language for pricing options. It is the main documented case of a model reshaping the market it describes, in both directions.
caseStudies.evidence: Compelling for options as one well-documented case, but MacKenzie himself says consistency with performativity does not prove it, and its general scope is debated.
caseStudies.plain: A formula for pricing options fit the market badly at first, then traders adopted it and prices moved to match, until the 1987 crash.

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory

caseStudies.label: Apartheid race classification
caseStudies.summary: Under the 1950 Population Registration Act and Group Areas Act, South Africans were classified by racial group, initially from 1951 census returns, using criteria of appearance and general acceptance and repute and devices such as the pencil test. About 100,000 people applied for reclassification, appeals averaged 14 months, and in 1984 alone 795 people were reclassified (518 from coloured to white); in one family, twins were classified differently. Bowker and Star analyze it in Sorting Things Out (ch. 6); it is classification torque at its most extreme: categories overriding family, biography and self-identification.
caseStudies.evidence: Historical and documentary evidence from Bowker and Star's Sorting Things Out (ch. 6); a case study, not an experiment.
caseStudies.plain: South Africa's government sorted every person into a legal race category that decided where they could live and work, even splitting families.

caseStudies.label: Leibniz's dy/dx and the British lag
caseStudies.summary: After the Newton-Leibniz priority dispute, British mathematicians kept Newton's fluxional dot notation while the Continent built analysis on Leibniz's differentials, whose symbols encode the chain rule and change of variables. Woodhouse introduced Leibniz notation in 1803, the Analytical Society (Babbage, Herschel, Peacock) formed in 1812, Peacock used continental notation in the 1817 Tripos, and it was widely adopted by about 1830. It illustrates a notation setting the cost of operations, and loyalty keeping a weaker one in place.
caseStudies.evidence: A good illustration but multi-causal: notation, Newton's geometric methods and the post-dispute breakdown of exchange all contributed to the British lag.
caseStudies.plain: British mathematicians stayed loyal to Newton's way of writing calculus, while the rest of Europe used Leibniz's handier symbols and pulled ahead.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought

caseStudies.label: The Asian disease problem
caseStudies.summary: Tversky and Kahneman (Science, 1981) found that 72% of subjects chose a certain program when outcomes were described as lives saved, while 78% chose a risky program when the identical outcomes were described as lives lost. Many Labs (2014) reproduced the reversal in 31 of 36 samples (6,344 participants), with none reversed, and a 2020 survey of 88,181 people in 47 countries found it again. It is a robustly replicated demonstration that logically equivalent descriptions produce different choices.
caseStudies.evidence: Robust: replicated in 31 of 36 Many Labs samples, with a smaller effect than in the 1981 original, and found again across 47 countries.
caseStudies.plain: Describe the same outcomes as lives saved or as lives lost, and most people switch which plan they choose.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought

caseStudies.label: Russian blues
caseStudies.summary: Russian obligatorily distinguishes lighter blue (goluboy) from darker blue (siniy). Winawer et al. (PNAS, 2007) found Russian speakers discriminated two blues faster when they fell into different Russian categories; the advantage was eliminated by a verbal dual task but not a spatial one, and English speakers showed no category advantage. It shows a language category speeding a perceptual judgment only while language is active.
caseStudies.evidence: Among the better-supported linguistic-relativity results, but the effect is 'online' and removable by verbal interference, and other specific findings in the field are fragile.
caseStudies.plain: Russian has separate words for light blue and dark blue, and its speakers tell those shades apart faster, unless a word task interferes.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall

caseStudies.label: Pirahã and exact number
caseStudies.summary: Pirahã has no stable word even for 'one'. Frank, Everett, Fedorenko and Gibson (Cognition, 2008) found Pirahã speakers matched large exact quantities perfectly when objects stayed visible but were inaccurate on tasks requiring memory, and concluded that number words are a cognitive technology for tracking exact quantities across time, space and modality rather than a change to underlying number representation. It is the clearest statement of the weak position: a framework is a tool that extends some capacities, not a cage.
caseStudies.evidence: One published study (Cognition, 2008); it supports the weak view of language as a tool and counts against the strong view that a language fixes what its speakers can think.
caseStudies.plain: A people whose language has no number words can still match exact quantities they can see, but slip once the task needs memory.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall

caseStudies.label: Prompt formatting and the 76-point swing
caseStudies.summary: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr (ICLR 2024) found that meaning-preserving changes to prompt formatting (separators, spacing, capitalization) produced performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points for LLaMA-2-13B, with a median spread of 7.5 points and about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks and several open-source models. Format performance only weakly correlated between models, and sensitivity persisted with larger models, more few-shot examples and instruction tuning. They recommend reporting ranges across plausible formats.
caseStudies.evidence: A direct measurement across 50+ tasks and several open-source models in few-shot settings; the 76-point figure is the maximum for one model, against a median spread of 7.5 points.
caseStudies.plain: Changing only spacing, separators or capital letters in the wording given to an AI model moved its test accuracy by as much as 76 points.

passages.section: The clearest case is a machine

caseStudies.label: The DSM and RDoC
caseStudies.summary: On 29 April 2013, weeks before DSM-5 appeared, NIMH Director Thomas Insel wrote in 'Transforming Diagnosis' that the DSM's strength is reliability and its weakness a lack of validity, because its diagnoses rest on consensus about symptom clusters rather than objective laboratory measures. He announced that NIMH would re-orient research away from DSM categories toward the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC). The episode shows a classification shaping which research questions get asked and funded.
caseStudies.evidence: A documented statement by the NIMH director, not a measured effect; RDoC was a research framework, not a clinical replacement for the DSM.
caseStudies.plain: Psychiatry's manual defines illnesses by agreed lists of symptoms, and in 2013 a US research institute said its studies would move away from them.

caseStudies.label: QWERTY and the disputed lock-in story
caseStudies.summary: Paul David's 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY' (1985) made the keyboard layout the standard example of path dependence: an early choice entrenched by network effects and sunk investment, with typing schools training on QWERTY as the early adoption mechanism. Liebowitz and Margolis ('The Fable of the Keys', 1990) argued that the evidence for the rival Dvorak layout's superiority is scant, suspect and traceable largely to Dvorak himself; defenders reply that David never claimed a remediable market failure. The concept of path dependence is accepted; this example of it is disputed.
caseStudies.evidence: The lock-in story is disputed even though path dependence as a concept is not; use it to illustrate coordination lock-in, not proven inefficiency.
caseStudies.plain: The standard keyboard layout is the best-known example of an early choice that stuck, though whether a better layout really lost is disputed.

caseStudies.label: Chess experts and the Einstellung effect
caseStudies.summary: Bilalić, McLeod and Gobet (Cognition, 2008) showed that chess experts who had found a familiar solution reported searching for a better one while their eye movements kept returning to board regions tied to the familiar solution. Sheridan and Reingold (PLOS ONE, 2013) found a boundary condition: when the familiar move was an outright blunder rather than merely suboptimal, all the experts avoided it. It shows attention staying anchored to a known solution, even in experts.
caseStudies.evidence: Robust, with a known boundary condition: when the familiar move was an outright blunder, all of the experts avoided it.
caseStudies.plain: Chess experts who had found a familiar solution said they were hunting for a better one, while their eyes kept returning to the old one.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall

caseStudies.label: Crime as beast, crime as virus
caseStudies.summary: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (PLOS ONE, 2011) found that participants who read that crime was a 'beast' preying on a city favored enforcement more than those who read it was a 'virus' infecting the city, though both groups saw the same statistics; the effect depended on the metaphor appearing early. Steen, Reijnierse and Burgers (2014) argued it was smaller than claimed and sensitive to coding choices, while a German-language replication (Scientific Data, 2016) reproduced it. It is the best-known experimental test of conceptual metaphor theory.
caseStudies.evidence: Real but smaller and more conditional than first reported: contested by Steen and colleagues, partly vindicated by a German replication, and dependent on early placement and readers' prior attitudes.
caseStudies.plain: Readers told crime was a beast preying on a city favored tougher enforcement than readers told it was a virus, with the same statistics.

caseStudies.label: The Gaussian copula and 2008
caseStudies.summary: Felix Salmon's Wired article called David Li's Gaussian copula 'the formula that killed Wall Street'. MacKenzie and Spears (Social Studies of Science, 2014), drawing on 114 interviews, qualify this: within investment banks' culture of no-arbitrage modelling the copula was shared infrastructure, yielding implied correlations and giving traders and organizations a common way to agree on values and book profit and loss. Because it shaped coordination as much as estimates, its blind spot (correlation behavior in a housing-wide downturn) became systemic.
caseStudies.evidence: The 'killed Wall Street' claim is overstated; the careful account treats the model as one embedded component of an evaluation culture in a multi-causal crisis, not the sole cause.
caseStudies.plain: Investment banks shared one formula for agreeing on values and booking profits, so its blind spot about a housing-wide downturn became everyone's blind spot.

caseStudies.label: AI benchmarks as milestones
caseStudies.summary: Raji, Bender, Paullada, Denton and Hanna ('AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark', NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks, 2021) argue that AI research valorizes a small collection of influential benchmarks such as ImageNet and GLUE, treated as stand-ins for common problems framed as milestones toward general AI. Leaderboard gains get read as general progress, a construct-validity failure, and the benchmarks play a critical role in orienting research agendas. It shows a metric steering what a field counts as progress.
caseStudies.evidence: A published critique by researchers in the field, argued rather than measured; it fits the widely documented Goodhart and Campbell pattern but carries no effect size of its own.
caseStudies.plain: AI researchers compete on a small set of shared tests, and higher scores on them get read as progress toward general AI.
